explanations.explanation: David calls the LORD his shepherd and says he shall not want (Psalm 23:1). He trusts the LORD to care for him. That's a good place to begin, friend.
David isn't saying he won't earn anything. He says that with the LORD as his shepherd, he shall not want (Psalm 23:1). He's talking about the care he receives.
David doesn't say he'll never lose anything. He says the LORD is his shepherd and he shall not want (Psalm 23:1). His words point to the LORD's care.
Green pastures and quiet waters give me a picture of rest (Psalm 23:2). David says the LORD makes him lie down and leads him. I can almost hear my oven timer staying quiet for once.
That's a busy picture, but listen to David's words. He describes lying down in green pastures and being led beside quiet waters (Psalm 23:2). That sounds much more peaceful, friend.

David mentions a dark valley later, but here the picture is peaceful (Psalm 23:2, 4). The LORD makes him lie down in green pastures and leads him beside quiet waters (Psalm 23:2). Take a breath and picture that, friend.
David says the LORD restores his soul (Psalm 23:3). His care reaches deeper than the peaceful place David has just described (Psalm 23:2). That's a beautiful word to sit with, friend.
Look at the word David uses here. He says the LORD restores his soul (Psalm 23:3). That's care reaching right down to his soul.
David doesn't speak of his soul being weighed in this line. He says the LORD restores it (Psalm 23:3). The shepherd's care goes deep, friend.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: David says the LORD guides him in paths of righteousness for the sake of His name (Psalm 23:3). David gives us the reason right there. Those few words are worth noticing, friend.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: A flock fits the shepherd picture, so I can see why you'd pick it. But David says the LORD guides him for the sake of His name (Psalm 23:3). That's the reason this line gives.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: David's words take us somewhere else, friend. He says the LORD guides him in paths of righteousness for the sake of His name (Psalm 23:3). It's His name David points to here.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: David says he will fear no evil because the LORD is with him (Psalm 23:4). He speaks of walking through the valley, not avoiding it. In that shadow, he knows he is not alone.
David doesn't point to his own strength here. He says he will fear no evil because the LORD is with him (Psalm 23:4). His words turn our attention to the One beside him.
David doesn't say how long the valley is. He says he will fear no evil because the LORD is with him (Psalm 23:4). That presence is the reason he gives.
David says the LORD's rod and staff comfort him (Psalm 23:4). He speaks those words while describing the valley of the shadow of death. Even there, he speaks of comfort.

David does say the LORD's rod and staff comfort him (Psalm 23:4). He also says he will fear no evil because the LORD is with him. The valley is a heavy picture, friend, and David speaks of comfort there.
David says the LORD prepares a table before him (Psalm 23:5). The picture has shifted from a shepherd and sheep to a table set before David. There's plenty more to notice in that line, friend.
A tent isn't what David names here. He says the LORD prepares a table before him (Psalm 23:5). Picture the table as you read the rest of the verse.
David spoke of lying down earlier, so I can see the connection (Psalm 23:2). Here, though, he says the LORD prepares a table before him (Psalm 23:5). The picture has changed.
David says the LORD prepares the table in the presence of his enemies (Psalm 23:5). He doesn't say they are far away. That detail makes the picture worth a closer look.
David says the table is prepared in the presence of his enemies (Psalm 23:5). They aren't described as far away. Notice who prepares the table: the LORD.

An overflowing cup is a picture of plenty (Psalm 23:5). David describes it after saying the LORD prepares a table for him and anoints his head with oil. That cup isn't just full, friend. It's OVERFLOWING.
I can see how an overflowing cup might bring a spill to mind. But David's picture points to plenty, not carelessness (Psalm 23:5). He describes a cup filled beyond its rim.
David doesn't mention anyone rushing him. He says his cup overflows as he describes the LORD's care (Psalm 23:5). I think that picture speaks of plenty.
David says goodness and mercy will follow him all the days of his life (Psalm 23:6). That's quite a pair to have following you, friend. They're with him for all his days.
David names a different pair here. He says goodness and mercy will follow him all the days of his life (Psalm 23:6). Listen to the warmth in those words, friend.
Those are good things, but they aren't the words David uses in this line. He says goodness and mercy will follow him all the days of his life (Psalm 23:6). He looks ahead with confidence.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: David closes by saying he will dwell in the house of the LORD forever (Psalm 23:6). After speaking of goodness and mercy following him, he looks ahead to dwelling with the LORD. What a way to end the song, friend.
David doesn't name Hebron in this song. He says he will dwell in the house of the LORD forever (Psalm 23:6). That's where his final line takes us.
David isn't naming a land at the end of this song. He says he will dwell in the house of the LORD forever (Psalm 23:6). His last words look ahead to being there.
